cases.candidate_question: Assume only f is differentiable at a. Prove that f+g and f-g are differentiable at a for every real function g.
cases.mathematical_reason: Take a=0, f=0, g(x)=|x|. Neither sum nor difference is differentiable there; the hypothesis on g is essential.

cases.candidate_question: If f has derivative u and g has derivative v at a, is the product derivative u*g(a)?
cases.mathematical_reason: The missing term f(a)*v cannot be omitted. Take f(x)=1 and g(x)=x at a=0: proposed derivative is 0 but actual derivative is 1.

cases.candidate_question: Since f and g are differentiable at a, can I conclude f/g is continuous and differentiable at a even if g(a)=0?
cases.mathematical_reason: Take f=1, g(x)=x, a=0. Real inversion is discontinuous at zero even when division by zero is totalized; all quotient rules require a nonzero denominator value.

cases.candidate_question: Assume f and g are differentiable at a. Must f(g(x)) be differentiable or continuous at a?
cases.mathematical_reason: The outer hypothesis must hold at g(a). Let a=0, g(x)=x+1, and f(t)=1/(t-1), using totalized inversion at t=1. Both are differentiable at 0, but f(g(x))=1/x is discontinuous at 0.

cases.candidate_question: Can the constant c in the scalar multiple rule be replaced by an arbitrary real function c(x) without additional assumptions?
cases.mathematical_reason: For derivatives, c(x)=x and f(x)=1 gives derivative 1 rather than c(a)*0. For integrability, c(x)=1/x on (0,1] and f=1 yields a nonintegrable product, although f is integrable.

cases.candidate_question: If f has derivative u at a and v at b, must u=v?
cases.mathematical_reason: Uniqueness compares derivatives at the same point. For f(x)=x^2, a=0 and b=1 give u=0 and v=2.

cases.candidate_question: If f(a)=u for real u, does f have a derivative at a?
cases.mathematical_reason: A function value is not a HasDerivAt certificate. f(x)=|x| has f(0)=0 but is not differentiable at 0.

cases.candidate_question: Since f is continuous at a, can I infer differentiability at a?
cases.mathematical_reason: Continuity alone is insufficient. f(x)=|x| is continuous but not differentiable at a=0.

cases.candidate_question: If f is continuous or differentiable at a, does the same follow for f+g and f*g with no hypothesis on g?
cases.mathematical_reason: Take f=1 and g the indicator of {0}, with a=0. Both f+g and f*g are discontinuous at a. For failure of differentiability with continuous g, use g(x)=|x|.

cases.candidate_question: If f is differentiable at a, is |f| differentiable there even when f(a)=0?
cases.mathematical_reason: f(x)=x and a=0 gives |f(x)|=|x|, which has different left and right derivatives. Absolute value always preserves continuity but requires the nonzero-value premise for this differentiability rule.

cases.candidate_question: If f and g are interval-integrable on [a,b], can the addition/subtraction closure rule also prove integrability of f*g?
cases.mathematical_reason: No. On (0,1], take f(x)=g(x)=x^(-1/2), and assign value 0 at x=0. Both are integrable on [0,1], while f*g=1/x is not. Product integrability needs stronger assumptions.

cases.candidate_question: If f is interval-integrable on [a,b], can I conclude integrability on any other interval [c,d]?
cases.mathematical_reason: Endpoint reversal preserves the same interval, while joining requires a second integrability premise. f(x)=1/x is integrable on [1,2] but not on [0,1].

cases.candidate_question: If f is continuous at a single real point, is it interval-integrable between every pair of finite endpoints?
cases.mathematical_reason: A single continuity point gives no global control. f(x)=1/x is continuous at 1 but not integrable on [0,1]. The card assumes continuity at every real point.

cases.candidate_question: For arbitrary real functions b(x) and c(x), is the derivative of b(x)*x+c(x) equal to b(a)?
cases.mathematical_reason: The coefficients in the affine rule are constants. Taking b(x)=x and c(x)=0 gives x^2, with derivative 2a rather than a.

cases.candidate_question: Does the constant-function interval-integrability card prove integrability of f(x)=1 over all real numbers?
cases.mathematical_reason: The card quantifies finite real endpoints only. The integral of the constant 1 over the whole real line is infinite, so it is not integrable for real volume.

cases.candidate_question: If f is continuous everywhere, can its epsilon-delta radius be chosen independently of the base point over all of R?
cases.mathematical_reason: Pointwise continuity permits δ to depend on a. f(x)=x^2 is continuous everywhere but not uniformly continuous on R.
